days.title: Building the ML Data Foundation: S3 Data Lakes and File Formats

concepts.heading: S3 as the ML Data Lake Backbone
concepts.body: Most AWS ML pipelines root their data foundation in Amazon S3, organized into raw, curated, and feature-ready layers using bucket prefixes or separate buckets per stage. Raw data is landed unmodified for lineage and reprocessing, curated data has been cleaned and joined, and feature-ready data is shaped for direct consumption by training jobs. This layered structure lets teams reprocess from any stage without re-ingesting from source systems, and lets access controls tighten as data moves from raw to sensitive curated layers. On the exam, expect the layered S3 data lake pattern presented as the default answer whenever a question describes centralizing data from multiple sources for ML.

concepts.heading: Columnar Formats for Training Throughput
concepts.body: File format choice materially affects training speed: Parquet and ORC are columnar, compressed formats that let a training job read only the columns it needs, dramatically reducing I/O compared to row-based CSV or JSON when datasets are large. Columnar formats also support predicate pushdown and better compression ratios because similar values are stored contiguously. CSV remains useful for small datasets or human inspection, but any scenario mentioning slow data loading or hundreds of gigabytes of training data is a strong signal that converting to Parquet/ORC is the intended fix. Glue and Athena can perform this conversion as part of an ETL job.

concepts.heading: AWS Lake Formation for Governed Access
concepts.body: AWS Lake Formation centralizes permission management over data that lives in S3 and is cataloged in the Glue Data Catalog, enforcing fine-grained access at the column and row level rather than only at the bucket/prefix level that S3 bucket policies and IAM provide. This lets multiple teams query the same underlying tables while seeing only the columns or rows they are authorized for, which is critical when a data lake mixes PII with non-sensitive features. Lake Formation also simplifies cross-account data sharing without duplicating data. A scenario about multiple teams sharing one data lake but needing different column-level access points directly at Lake Formation rather than plain S3 policies.

concepts.heading: Storage Classes and Lifecycle Cost Control
concepts.body: S3 storage classes let teams match cost to access pattern: S3 Standard for actively used training data, S3 Standard-IA or Intelligent-Tiering for less frequently accessed curated data, and S3 Glacier classes for long-term archival of raw or historical datasets that compliance requires you to retain but rarely reprocess. Lifecycle policies automate the transition between classes based on object age, removing the need for manual cleanup. For ML workloads, a common pattern is keeping the current training window in Standard while archiving older training snapshots to a cheaper tier. Exam scenarios about reducing storage cost for infrequently accessed ML data map to lifecycle policies and storage class transitions.

examPoints: When a question describes slow training-job data loading caused by a row-based format like CSV or JSON on a multi-hundred-gigabyte dataset, the expected answer is converting the data to a columnar format such as Parquet or ORC.

When a question describes several teams sharing one S3-backed data lake but needing different column-level or row-level access to the same tables, the expected answer is AWS Lake Formation's fine-grained permissions rather than S3 bucket policies alone.

quiz.q: A team stores hundreds of gigabytes of labeled training data as CSV files in S3, and data scientists report that SageMaker training jobs spend a large fraction of runtime just reading input files. Which change would most directly reduce data loading time?
choices: Increase the number of CSV files without changing format
Convert the dataset to a columnar format such as Parquet
Store the data as plain text logs
quiz.explain: Parquet's columnar, compressed layout lets a training job read only the needed columns, cutting I/O compared to row-based CSV; XML and plain text would only add parsing overhead.

quiz.q: Several data science teams query the same S3 data lake, but the security team requires that each team see only the columns relevant to its project, not the entire schema. Which AWS service should manage this access model?
choices: S3 bucket policies applied uniformly to the whole bucket
AWS Lake Formation with column-level permissions
quiz.explain: Lake Formation provides fine-grained, column- and row-level permissions on top of the Glue Data Catalog, which bucket policies cannot express since they operate at the object/prefix level.

days.recap: Today's throughline: structure ML data in S3 by raw/curated/feature layers, prefer Parquet/ORC over CSV for training throughput, use Lake Formation for column-level governance, and apply lifecycle policies to control storage cost.

days.title: Ingesting Data at Scale: Batch ETL with Glue and Streaming with Kinesis

concepts.heading: AWS Glue for Serverless Batch ETL
concepts.body: AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service built around two core pieces: Glue Crawlers, which inspect data sources and infer schema automatically into the Glue Data Catalog, and Glue Jobs, which run Apache Spark-based transformations at scale without you managing clusters. Because Glue is serverless, it scales transparently with data volume and only bills for the compute actually consumed during a job run. Glue Studio provides a visual interface for building ETL jobs, while Glue also supports custom PySpark or Scala scripts for complex logic. Any scenario about periodically cleaning and loading large volumes of heterogeneous batch data into a data lake is a strong signal for Glue.

concepts.heading: Kinesis Data Streams for Real-Time Ingestion
concepts.body: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams ingests continuous, high-throughput streaming data such as clickstreams, IoT telemetry, or application logs, making it the natural source when an ML pipeline needs to compute features or trigger predictions in near real time. Data is organized into shards, each providing fixed read/write throughput, and consumers such as Kinesis Data Analytics or a Lambda function can process records as they arrive rather than waiting for a batch window. This differs fundamentally from Glue, which is designed for scheduled, bounded batch jobs rather than continuously flowing data. Exam scenarios describing immediate reaction to newly generated events point to Kinesis rather than batch ETL.

concepts.heading: Amazon MSK for Kafka-Based Pipelines
concepts.body: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka) is the right choice when an organization already has Kafka-based producers, consumers, or tooling and wants to migrate to a managed service without rewriting that ecosystem. MSK handles broker provisioning, patching, and replication while preserving full compatibility with the open-source Kafka API, unlike Kinesis which uses AWS-specific APIs and SDKs. Choosing between Kinesis and MSK on the exam usually comes down to whether the question emphasizes existing Kafka investment (MSK) or the simplest native AWS streaming service (Kinesis). Both can feed streaming features into a Feature Store's online store for low-latency serving.

concepts.heading: Choosing Batch vs. Streaming Ingestion
concepts.body: The decision between batch and streaming ingestion hinges on how quickly new data needs to influence predictions or training: periodic, large-volume processing where some latency is acceptable favors Glue-based batch ETL, while sub-second or near-real-time requirements favor Kinesis or MSK. Many production ML systems use both — Glue for daily or hourly refreshes of training datasets, and Kinesis for streaming features that update an online Feature Store. A common exam trap is choosing a streaming service for a workload that is actually just a large nightly batch job, which would be needlessly complex and costly compared to a scheduled Glue job. Cost, operational complexity, and freshness requirements should all factor into this choice.

examPoints: A scenario describing regularly scheduled cleansing and loading of large volumes of heterogeneous source data into a data lake signals AWS Glue's serverless batch ETL as the answer.

A scenario describing the need to transform freshly generated events into features immediately, such as clickstream or IoT data, signals Amazon Kinesis Data Streams (or MSK if an existing Kafka stack is mentioned) rather than a batch tool.

quiz.q: A company needs to periodically cleanse and load data from several heterogeneous on-premises and cloud sources into a centralized data lake for ML training, without managing any servers. Which service best fits this requirement?
quiz.explain: Glue provides serverless ETL with automatic schema discovery via Crawlers and Spark-based batch transformation jobs; Kinesis and MSK are built for continuous streaming, not scheduled batch loads.

quiz.q: An ML team needs to convert live clickstream events into features that update a model's inputs within seconds of the event occurring. Which service should ingest this data?
choices: Storing files in S3 on a schedule
quiz.explain: Kinesis Data Streams is designed for continuous, low-latency ingestion of streaming events, unlike Glue's batch-oriented model or Athena's on-demand query engine.

days.recap: Glue delivers serverless batch ETL with schema discovery via the Data Catalog, Kinesis Data Streams and MSK handle real-time and Kafka-based streaming respectively, and the batch-vs-streaming choice should be driven by how quickly new data must reach the model.

days.title: Centralizing Features: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store

concepts.heading: Solving Training-Serving Skew
concepts.body: SageMaker Feature Store exists primarily to eliminate training-serving skew, the problem where the feature computation logic used during model training differs subtly from the logic used at inference time, causing predictions to degrade in production even though offline evaluation looked fine. By storing feature definitions and values in one central repository that both training pipelines and real-time inference systems read from, teams guarantee that a feature like average purchase amount over 30 days is computed identically everywhere. This is one of the most exam-relevant reasons to reach for Feature Store rather than ad-hoc feature computation scattered across notebooks and application code. It also reduces duplicated feature engineering effort across teams working on related models.

concepts.heading: Online Store vs. Offline Store
concepts.body: Feature Store splits storage into two tiers with very different performance characteristics: the online store provides low-latency, low-millisecond lookups of the most recent feature values, purpose-built for real-time inference, while the offline store is backed by S3 and holds the full historical record of feature values, suited for training, batch scoring, and analytics. A single feature group can write to both stores simultaneously, so a streaming pipeline can update the online store for serving while the same data accumulates in the offline store for the next training run. Exam questions that mention needing both instant lookups for live predictions and large historical datasets for retraining point to using both stores together rather than choosing one over the other.

concepts.heading: Feature Groups, Record Identifiers, and Event Time
concepts.body: A feature group is the core organizational unit in Feature Store — a logical collection of related features that share a schema, such as all features describing a customer. Every record in a feature group is uniquely identified by a Record Identifier (e.g., customer ID) and timestamped with an Event Time, which together let the store retrieve the exact feature values that were valid at a given point in time. This time-travel capability is essential for correctly reconstructing point-in-time-accurate training datasets and avoiding accidental data leakage from future values. Feature groups can be created via the SageMaker SDK or console and integrate directly with Data Wrangler flows for feature engineering.

concepts.heading: Cross-Team Feature Reuse and Governance
concepts.body: Beyond consistency, Feature Store enables organizational reuse: once a feature like customer lifetime value is engineered and validated by one team, other teams building different models can discover and reuse it rather than re-deriving it from raw data, cutting duplicated engineering effort and improving consistency across a company's ML models. Feature Store also integrates with SageMaker's built-in encryption and access control, so sensitive features can be governed the same way other SageMaker resources are. In an exam scenario about reducing duplicate feature engineering work across multiple model teams, Feature Store's shared feature groups are the expected answer over each team building isolated pipelines.

examPoints: A scenario where feature values computed for training differ from those computed for live inference and predictions suffer — the training-serving skew pattern — signals SageMaker Feature Store as the fix.

A scenario requiring both low-latency lookups for real-time inference and large historical datasets for retraining points to using the Feature Store's online store and offline store together, not one alone.

quiz.q: A team observes that a fraud-detection model performs well in offline evaluation but poorly once deployed, and investigation reveals the real-time serving code computes a key feature slightly differently than the training pipeline. What is the best long-term fix?
choices: Add more training data without changing the pipeline
Centralize feature computation and storage in SageMaker Feature Store so training and inference share the same values
quiz.explain: This is a textbook training-serving skew problem, and Feature Store is designed specifically to guarantee training and inference use identical feature definitions and values.

quiz.q: Which Feature Store component is designed to serve the most recent feature values with the low latency needed for real-time inference?
quiz.explain: The online store is optimized for low-latency point lookups used by live inference, while the offline store, backed by S3, serves historical/batch use cases.

days.recap: Feature Store guarantees training-serving consistency across teams, splits storage into a low-latency online store and a historical S3-backed offline store, and organizes data into feature groups keyed by record identifier and event time.

days.title: Feature Engineering Techniques: Scaling, Encoding, and Handling Imbalance

concepts.heading: Normalization and Standardization
concepts.body: Feature scaling puts numeric features on comparable ranges so that gradient-descent-based algorithms converge faster and more stably, and so that distance-based algorithms like k-NN or k-means aren't dominated by features with naturally larger magnitudes. Min-max scaling rescales values into a fixed range such as 0 to 1 and is sensitive to outliers since a single extreme value stretches the whole range, while z-score standardization transforms values to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 and handles outliers somewhat better. Tree-based models such as XGBoost are largely insensitive to feature scale, so scaling matters most for linear models, neural networks, and distance-based methods. Scaling parameters must be fit only on training data and then applied unchanged to validation and test data to avoid leakage.

concepts.heading: Encoding Categorical Variables
concepts.body: Categorical features need numeric encoding before most algorithms can use them: one-hot encoding creates a binary column per category and works well when the number of categories is small, label encoding assigns an integer to each category and is appropriate for ordinal variables with a natural order, and target encoding replaces a category with a statistic of the target variable and is preferred when cardinality is very high because one-hot encoding would otherwise create an explosion of sparse columns. Embeddings, learned during neural network training, are another high-cardinality option common in deep learning pipelines. The exam frequently frames thousands of categories as the cue for target encoding or embeddings rather than one-hot encoding.

concepts.heading: Handling Missing Values
concepts.body: Missing data can be addressed several ways depending on why it's missing and how much of it there is: imputation replaces missing values with the mean, median, or mode of the column; treating missingness itself as a separate category preserves potentially meaningful signal; and dropping columns or rows is reasonable only when missingness is extensive and the feature/record carries little other information. The right strategy is domain-dependent — median imputation is more robust than mean imputation when a column has outliers, since the mean is pulled by extreme values while the median is not. SageMaker Data Wrangler provides built-in transforms for each of these imputation strategies without custom code.

concepts.heading: Addressing Class Imbalance
concepts.body: Imbalanced datasets, where one class vastly outnumbers another (fraud detection is the classic exam example), cause models to default toward predicting the majority class and score deceptively well on accuracy while failing to detect the minority class that actually matters. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) generates synthetic minority-class examples by interpolating between existing ones rather than simply duplicating them, undersampling reduces the majority class to rebalance the dataset at the cost of discarding data, and class weighting penalizes the model more heavily for misclassifying minority-class examples without altering the dataset itself. The right choice depends on how much data can be safely discarded and whether the algorithm supports class weights natively, as XGBoost and many SageMaker built-in algorithms do.

examPoints: A scenario describing a categorical feature with thousands of distinct values that would explode into too many columns under one-hot encoding signals target encoding or embeddings as the answer.

A scenario describing a severely imbalanced dataset, such as fraud detection where positive cases are under 1% of records, signals SMOTE oversampling or class weighting rather than relying on accuracy or leaving the data unmodified.

quiz.q: A categorical feature representing product SKU has over 50,000 distinct values, and one-hot encoding it would create an unmanageably wide and sparse feature matrix. What is the more scalable encoding approach?
choices: Use target encoding or a learned embedding
Drop the feature without further analysis
Use label encoding as if it were ordinal
quiz.explain: Target encoding or embeddings compress high-cardinality categorical data into a small number of informative numeric features without the dimensionality explosion one-hot encoding would cause.

quiz.q: In a fraud-detection dataset, fraudulent transactions make up only 0.2% of records, and a naive model achieves 99.8% accuracy by always predicting 'not fraud.' What technique most directly addresses this imbalance during training?
choices: Leave the dataset unchanged since accuracy is high
Apply SMOTE oversampling or class weighting to emphasize the minority class
quiz.explain: SMOTE oversampling or class weighting forces the model to pay attention to the rare minority class instead of being dominated by the majority class, unlike relying on the misleading accuracy metric.

days.recap: Feature engineering combines scaling (min-max vs. z-score) for numeric features, encoding strategy chosen by categorical cardinality, a missing-value strategy matched to the cause of missingness, and imbalance techniques like SMOTE, undersampling, or class weighting for skewed classes.

days.title: Visual Data Preparation with SageMaker Data Wrangler

concepts.heading: Low-Code Data Exploration and Transformation
concepts.body: SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a visual, notebook-integrated interface with over 300 pre-built transformations, letting data scientists explore, clean, and reshape data with minimal custom code. Transformations include type conversion, encoding, scaling, text processing, and time-series-specific operations, all applied through a point-and-click flow rather than hand-written Pandas or PySpark. This dramatically compresses the time typically spent on data preparation, which is widely cited as the most time-consuming phase of an ML project. Any exam scenario describing a data scientist who wants to explore and transform data with minimal code or through a visual interface is describing Data Wrangler.

concepts.heading: Automated Data Quality and Insights Reports
concepts.body: Data Wrangler's Data Quality and Insights report automatically analyzes a dataset for missing values, outliers, class imbalance, feature correlations, and other common data problems, presenting the findings visually without the analyst having to write diagnostic code by hand. This report acts as an early-warning system before modeling begins, flagging issues that would otherwise only surface after a confusing round of poor model performance. Because this diagnostic step is largely automated, it's a fast way to triage a new dataset's quality before investing time in feature engineering. The exam associates automatically diagnosing missing values, outliers, or imbalance specifically with this report rather than manual EDA.

concepts.heading: Exporting Flows into Production Pipelines
concepts.body: A Data Wrangler flow — the recorded sequence of transformations applied interactively — isn't a dead end for prototyping; it can be exported directly into a SageMaker Pipelines processing step, turning an interactive exploration session into a reproducible, automatically re-runnable production data pipeline. This closes the gap between what a data scientist did once in a notebook and what actually runs on a schedule in production, without requiring the transformations to be manually re-implemented in code. Exported flows can also be scheduled or triggered as part of a larger MLOps pipeline. This export path is why Data Wrangler pairs so naturally with SageMaker Pipelines on the exam.

concepts.heading: Connecting Multiple Data Sources
concepts.body: Data Wrangler connects directly to sources such as S3, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon EMR, allowing joins, aggregations, and other multi-source transformations to be built visually without first consolidating everything manually into one location. This is particularly useful when feature data is scattered across a data warehouse, a data lake, and a big-data cluster, since Data Wrangler can pull from all three into a single unified flow. Because these connections use existing IAM permissions, no additional data movement or duplication is required to start exploring. This multi-source capability distinguishes Data Wrangler from tools that only operate on a single already-consolidated dataset.

examPoints: A scenario describing a data scientist wanting to explore and transform data quickly with minimal custom code, through a visual interface, points to SageMaker Data Wrangler.
A scenario asking for automatic detection of missing values, outliers, or class imbalance in a dataset points to Data Wrangler's Data Quality and Insights report rather than manual analysis.

quiz.q: A data scientist wants to visually explore, clean, and transform a raw dataset with as little hand-written code as possible before training a model. Which tool is purpose-built for this?
choices: Direct SQL queries in Athena only
quiz.explain: Data Wrangler offers a visual interface with 300+ pre-built transformations specifically to minimize hand-written code during data preparation.

quiz.q: Before starting feature engineering, a team wants an automatic diagnostic of missing values, outliers, and class imbalance in a new dataset. Which Data Wrangler feature provides this?
choices: Exporting a flow to SageMaker Pipelines
The Data Quality and Insights report
quiz.explain: The Data Quality and Insights report automatically analyzes and visualizes exactly these data quality issues before modeling begins.

days.recap: Data Wrangler enables low-code, visual data exploration across 300+ transforms, automatically surfaces data quality issues through its Insights report, connects to multiple source systems, and can export its flow directly into a reproducible SageMaker Pipelines step.

days.title: Detecting Bias and Explaining Models with SageMaker Clarify

concepts.heading: Pre-Training vs. Post-Training Bias
concepts.body: SageMaker Clarify measures two distinct kinds of bias: pre-training bias, which looks only at the training data itself, and post-training bias, which examines whether a trained model's predictions treat different groups unfairly even if the raw data looked balanced. Checking for pre-training bias early can prevent building a model on a flawed dataset in the first place, while post-training bias catches problems that emerge from how the algorithm itself learned patterns. Both types of analysis integrate into SageMaker Processing jobs and can run as part of an automated pipeline before a model is approved for deployment. On the exam, checking data before modeling maps to pre-training metrics and checking model predictions after training maps to post-training metrics.

concepts.heading: Bias Metrics and Demographic Group Comparison
concepts.body: Clarify computes concrete bias metrics such as Class Imbalance (disproportionate representation of a facet, like a demographic group, in the dataset) and Difference in Positive Proportions in Labels (whether one group has a systematically different rate of the favorable outcome in the ground-truth labels). These metrics quantify disparities between groups rather than relying on subjective judgment, giving compliance and fairness reviews an objective, reproducible basis. Reports can be generated automatically and reviewed by both technical and non-technical stakeholders. Exam scenarios that mention checking whether specific demographic groups are underrepresented or treated unfairly describe exactly this bias-metric functionality.

concepts.heading: Explainability with SHAP Values
concepts.body: Clarify's explainability feature uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, a game-theory-based method that attributes a portion of each individual prediction to each input feature, quantifying how much that feature pushed the prediction up or down relative to a baseline. This addresses the black-box criticism of complex models like gradient-boosted trees or neural networks by making individual predictions interpretable, which matters both for debugging unexpected predictions and for regulatory requirements that demand explainable decisions. SHAP values can be aggregated across many predictions to show overall feature importance for the whole model, not just single predictions. A question asking to quantitatively explain why the model made a specific prediction is asking for SHAP-based explainability.

concepts.heading: Data Integrity Checks Before Modeling
concepts.body: Beyond bias and explainability, good practice requires validating basic data integrity before modeling: schema consistency, duplicate record detection, and label noise checks that identify records that appear to be mislabeled. These checks are cheap to run and catch problems that would otherwise silently degrade model quality and be much harder to diagnose after the fact. Data Wrangler's Data Quality report and Clarify's bias analysis complement each other here — one focuses on general data health, the other on fairness specifically. Treating these checks as a mandatory pre-modeling gate, rather than an afterthought, is a recurring theme across the exam's data-preparation domain.

examPoints: A scenario about checking, before any model is trained, whether the training data itself is skewed toward or against a demographic group signals SageMaker Clarify's pre-training bias analysis.
A scenario asking to quantitatively explain how much each input feature contributed to a specific prediction signals SHAP-based explainability in SageMaker Clarify.

quiz.q: Before training a loan-approval model, a compliance team wants to verify whether the historical training data itself already shows a skewed approval rate between demographic groups. Which capability addresses this?
choices: Train the model first, then investigate
quiz.explain: Pre-training bias analysis in Clarify examines the raw data itself, before a model exists, for exactly this kind of representational or label skew.

quiz.q: Regulators require a lender to explain, for a specific rejected loan application, how much each factor contributed to the model's decision. Which Clarify feature provides this?
quiz.explain: SHAP values attribute a quantitative contribution to each feature for an individual prediction, which is exactly the per-decision explanation regulators are asking for.

days.recap: Clarify separates pre-training bias (in the raw data) from post-training bias (in model predictions), quantifies both with concrete metrics, explains individual predictions via SHAP values, and works alongside basic data-integrity checks like schema consistency and duplicate detection.

days.title: Splitting and Labeling Data: Train/Validation/Test and SageMaker Ground Truth

concepts.heading: The Purpose of Train/Validation/Test Splits
concepts.body: Splitting data into training, validation, and test sets serves distinct purposes that must not be blurred: the training set fits model parameters, the validation set guides hyperparameter tuning and model selection decisions, and the test set is reserved strictly for a single final performance estimate after all tuning is complete. Using the test set repeatedly during development effectively turns it into a second validation set and produces an overly optimistic estimate of real-world performance — a subtle form of data leakage. A common split ratio is 70/15/15 or 80/10/10, though the right ratio depends on total dataset size. Exam questions about data leakage often trace back to test data being used, even indirectly, during model development.

concepts.heading: Time-Aware Splitting for Time-Series Data
concepts.body: For time-series or any temporally ordered data, a random train/test split leaks future information into training, because rows that would only be available after the prediction point end up training the model that must predict earlier points. The correct approach is a chronological split — training on older data and testing on the most recent period — which better mirrors how the model will actually be used at inference time. A model evaluated with a random split on time-series data can appear to perform excellently offline while performing far worse once deployed, because the evaluation was never realistic. Any scenario describing surprisingly poor real-world performance despite strong offline metrics on time-ordered data is describing this leakage pattern.

concepts.heading: SageMaker Ground Truth for Human Labeling
concepts.body: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth manages human-in-the-loop data labeling workflows for tasks like image classification, object detection, text classification, and semantic segmentation, offering a choice of workforce: a private workforce of your own employees or vetted third-party labeling vendors (the Amazon Mechanical Turk public crowd option ended when Mechanical Turk closed on 2026-09-29). Ground Truth's active learning capability trains an auxiliary model during the labeling process that automatically labels examples it's confident about, sending only ambiguous cases to human labelers, which substantially reduces labeling cost and turnaround time as the process continues. This blend of automation and human judgment is what distinguishes Ground Truth from purely manual labeling tools. A scenario about labeling large volumes of unlabeled images or text at lower cost is the classic Ground Truth cue.

concepts.heading: Cross-Validation for Small Datasets
concepts.body: When a dataset is too small to comfortably support a single held-out validation set without wasting data, k-fold cross-validation repeatedly splits the data into k different train/validation partitions, trains and evaluates the model k times, and averages the resulting metric to produce a more stable and trustworthy estimate of generalization performance than a single split would give. This comes at the cost of k times the training compute, which matters for expensive models but is usually manageable for smaller datasets where cross-validation is most valuable. Stratified k-fold, which preserves class proportions in every fold, is preferred when classes are imbalanced. The exam frames cross-validation as the answer whenever limited data and reliable performance estimate appear together.

examPoints: A scenario describing a time-series model whose real-world performance is much worse than its offline evaluation, caused by a random rather than chronological train/test split, signals the fix of preserving temporal order in the split.

A scenario describing a large volume of unlabeled images or text that needs human-applied labels signals Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth, especially when cost-efficient labeling at scale via active learning is emphasized.

quiz.q: A retailer builds a monthly sales forecasting model, randomly splitting historical data into train and test sets. In production, forecast accuracy is far worse than the offline test metrics suggested. What most likely explains this?
choices: The model architecture is too simple
A random split leaked future information into training instead of preserving chronological order
There is too much training data
quiz.explain: Time-series data must be split chronologically; a random split lets the model train on data that temporally follows what it's being tested on, producing an unrealistically optimistic offline evaluation.

quiz.q: A company has millions of unlabeled product images and needs a managed workflow to have humans apply classification labels at scale and lower cost. Which service fits this need?
quiz.explain: Ground Truth manages human labeling workflows, including active learning to reduce the number of items that require a human labeler.

days.recap: Train/validation/test sets each serve a distinct purpose and must stay separated to avoid leakage, time-series data requires chronological rather than random splitting, Ground Truth manages scalable human labeling with active learning, and cross-validation improves reliability when data is limited.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: The ML Data Preparation Toolkit

concepts.heading: The Domain 1 Data Pipeline End to End
concepts.body: Domain 1's services form a natural pipeline: data lands and is organized in S3, gets ingested and cleaned via Glue for batch or Kinesis/MSK for streaming, becomes reusable model inputs through Feature Store after feature engineering techniques like scaling, encoding, and imbalance handling, can be explored and transformed visually with Data Wrangler, gets checked for bias and integrity with Clarify, and finally is split and, where needed, labeled with Ground Truth before modeling begins. Seeing this as one continuous pipeline rather than seven disconnected services is the fastest way to recognize which stage a scenario question is really asking about. Domain 1 carries the largest exam weight at 28%, so fluency across this whole chain pays off disproportionately.

concepts.heading: Matching Data Problems to the Right Tool
concepts.body: The recurring exam skill in Domain 1 is mapping a described data problem to the one correct tool: slow training reads from CSV map to Parquet conversion, fine-grained multi-team access maps to Lake Formation, inconsistent train/serve features map to Feature Store, high-cardinality categorical variables map to target encoding, severe class imbalance maps to SMOTE or class weighting, unfair or skewed training data maps to Clarify, unlabeled raw data maps to Ground Truth, and time-series evaluation leakage maps to chronological splitting. Practicing this problem-to-service mapping in both directions builds the pattern recognition the exam actually tests. Most Domain 1 wrong answers are technically real AWS services, just ones solving an adjacent but different problem.

concepts.heading: Batch vs. Streaming and Governance as Cross-Cutting Themes
concepts.body: Two themes cut across nearly every Domain 1 service: the batch-versus-streaming decision and the governance-versus-flexibility tradeoff between Lake Formation's fine-grained control and simpler but coarser S3 bucket policies. Recognizing these two axes helps eliminate distractor answers quickly, since a wrong answer often proposes the right general category of service but the wrong latency profile or the wrong level of access granularity. Keeping a running mental checklist of whether a scenario is batch or streaming, and fine-grained or coarse-grained, while reading a question narrows most Domain 1 questions to two candidates almost immediately.

concepts.heading: From Raw Data to Model-Ready Input
concepts.body: Zooming out, every Domain 1 topic exists to answer one question: how does raw, messy, real-world data become a trustworthy, well-structured input a model can learn from? Storage and ingestion answer where data lives and how it arrives, feature engineering and Feature Store answer how it's shaped and kept consistent, Clarify and data-integrity checks answer whether it can be trusted, and splitting and labeling answer how it's organized for training and honest evaluation. Keeping this single guiding question in mind while reviewing prevents the eight days of Domain 1 material from feeling like an unrelated service list.

examPoints: When a Domain 1 scenario doesn't obviously match one service, first classify it as batch vs. streaming and training-time vs. inference-time, which usually narrows the answer to two candidates.
Distractor answers in Domain 1 are frequently real AWS services that solve a related but distinct problem, so verify the specific requirement (bias vs. quality vs. skew vs. leakage) before selecting.

quiz.q: Which service directly resolves the problem of a model performing well offline but poorly in production because training and inference compute a key feature differently?
quiz.explain: Feature Store guarantees training and inference reuse identical feature definitions and values, directly preventing this training-serving skew.

quiz.q: Which technique specifically augments the minority class in a severely imbalanced classification dataset by generating synthetic examples?
quiz.explain: SMOTE synthesizes new minority-class examples by interpolating between existing ones, which one-hot encoding, standardization, and target encoding do not do.

days.recap: Domain 1 wraps up as one continuous pipeline — store (S3) to ingest (Glue/Kinesis) to feature (Feature Store/Data Wrangler) to validate (Clarify) to split/label (Ground Truth) — and the exam mainly tests matching a described data problem to the single correct stage.

days.title: Choosing a Modeling Approach: Built-in Algorithms, Custom Models, and AutoML

concepts.heading: SageMaker Built-in Algorithms
concepts.body: SageMaker ships a library of built-in algorithms — XGBoost, Linear Learner, K-Means, and others — that are pre-implemented, optimized for distributed training on SageMaker infrastructure, and ready to use by simply pointing them at data in S3 and specifying hyperparameters. This drastically lowers the barrier to getting a working model quickly, since there's no need to write or debug custom training code, and the algorithms are tuned to work well with SageMaker's distributed training and Automatic Model Tuning features out of the box. Built-in algorithms are the default choice for well-understood, standard problems like tabular classification/regression or common clustering tasks. The tradeoff is less flexibility for highly specialized architectures.

concepts.heading: Bring Your Own Container or Script
concepts.body: When a problem needs a specific architecture or framework — a custom neural network in PyTorch or TensorFlow, or a novel training loop — SageMaker supports Bring Your Own Script, using a SageMaker-managed framework container with your own training code, or Bring Your Own Container, a fully custom Docker image implementing the required training and inference interface. This approach gives maximum control and is necessary whenever built-in algorithms can't express the modeling approach required, at the cost of more setup and ongoing maintenance responsibility. Custom containers still benefit from SageMaker's managed infrastructure: distributed training, Spot instances, and Model Registry integration are all still available. The exam frames no built-in algorithm fits this specialized deep learning architecture as the cue for BYOC/BYOS.

concepts.heading: SageMaker Autopilot for AutoML
concepts.body: SageMaker Autopilot automates the entire modeling workflow — data preprocessing, algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning, and model ranking — from just a dataset and a target column, producing multiple candidate models along with full visibility into the pipeline it generated via generated notebooks rather than acting as an opaque black box. This is especially valuable for teams without deep ML expertise who need a strong baseline quickly, or for experienced teams who want an automated baseline to beat with custom modeling effort. Autopilot supports both tabular classification/regression tasks and can hand off its best candidate for further manual tuning. Exam scenarios describing limited ML expertise and a need for a fast, automated baseline point to Autopilot.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Approach
concepts.body: The decision among these three approaches generally follows problem standardization and team expertise: standard, well-defined problems needing fast results favor built-in algorithms or Autopilot, while unusual architectures, cutting-edge research techniques, or highly specific business logic favor custom models. It's also common to start with Autopilot or a built-in algorithm to establish a baseline, then invest in a custom model only if the baseline doesn't meet requirements, avoiding premature complexity. The exam rewards recognizing that fastest path to a working model almost never means jumping straight to a custom deep learning architecture when a built-in algorithm or Autopilot would suffice.

examPoints: A scenario describing a team with limited ML expertise that needs a fast, automated baseline model signals SageMaker Autopilot.
A scenario describing a standard classification or regression problem needing a quick, well-tested algorithm signals a SageMaker built-in algorithm such as XGBoost rather than a custom-built model.

quiz.q: A small startup with no dedicated data scientists needs to quickly produce a working baseline model from a tabular dataset with minimal manual effort. What is the best starting point?
choices: Implement a custom deep learning architecture from scratch
Use SageMaker Autopilot for automated preprocessing, algorithm selection, and tuning
Skip modeling and use only rule-based logic
Manually try hundreds of algorithm and hyperparameter combinations
quiz.explain: Autopilot automates the full modeling workflow end to end, making it the fastest path to a working baseline for teams without deep ML expertise.

quiz.q: A team needs to quickly build a well-tested model for a standard binary classification problem on tabular data. Which is the most efficient starting point?
choices: Design a custom neural network from scratch
Use a SageMaker built-in algorithm such as XGBoost
Collect more data indefinitely before modeling
quiz.explain: Built-in algorithms are optimized, pre-implemented solutions ideal for standard problems, avoiding the extra time and risk of custom architecture development.

days.recap: Built-in algorithms offer fast starts for standard problems, Bring Your Own Container/Script gives full control for specialized architectures, and Autopilot automates the entire pipeline for AutoML baselines — the choice hinges on problem standardization and team expertise.

days.title: SageMaker Training Jobs: Distributed Training and Managed Spot Training

concepts.heading: How a SageMaker Training Job Runs
concepts.body: A SageMaker training job launches a specified number and type of managed instances, pulls a training container, runs your training script against data staged from S3, writes model artifacts back to S3, and then automatically terminates the instances, meaning you pay only for the actual training duration rather than for infrastructure sitting idle before or after the job. This ephemeral-by-default model contrasts with keeping a persistent training cluster running, and is a core reason SageMaker training is cost-effective compared to self-managed EC2/EMR clusters for training. Training job configuration includes instance type/count, hyperparameters, input data channels, and output location, all specified through the SageMaker API or SDK.

concepts.heading: Data Parallelism vs. Model Parallelism
concepts.body: When a single instance can't train a model fast enough or can't fit it in memory, SageMaker supports two distributed training strategies: data parallelism replicates the entire model on multiple instances and splits the training data across them, aggregating gradients periodically, appropriate when the model fits on one device but the dataset or desired training speed demands more compute. Model parallelism instead splits a single very large model's layers or parameters across multiple devices, which is necessary when the model itself is too large to fit in a single GPU's memory, as with very large language models. SageMaker's distributed training libraries support both patterns natively. A question mentioning a model too large for one GPU's memory is specifically pointing at model parallelism, not data parallelism.

concepts.heading: Managed Spot Training and Checkpointing
concepts.body: Managed Spot Training runs training jobs on spare EC2 capacity at up to a 90% discount versus on-demand pricing, but Spot instances can be reclaimed by AWS with short notice, so training jobs must periodically write checkpoints, typically to S3, so an interrupted job can resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch. SageMaker handles the interruption and resumption logic automatically once checkpointing is configured, making Spot training a low-risk way to substantially cut training cost for jobs that can tolerate some interruption-driven delay. This combination, deep discount plus automatic resumption, is why the exam treats reduce training cost while tolerating interruption as the Managed Spot Training plus checkpointing pattern specifically, not just use Spot instances.

concepts.heading: Input Data Modes: File, Pipe, and FastFile
concepts.body: How training data moves from S3 to the training instance affects startup time and throughput: File mode downloads the entire dataset to local disk before training starts, which is simple but adds startup latency proportional to dataset size; Pipe mode streams data directly into the training algorithm as it downloads, overlapping I/O with computation and cutting startup time significantly for large datasets; and FastFile mode exposes S3 objects as if they were local files while only fetching the bytes actually accessed, combining file-like semantics with on-demand streaming. Pipe and FastFile modes matter most for very large datasets where File mode's upfront download would waste significant time before training even begins. The exam associates reduce time-to-start for large training datasets with Pipe or FastFile mode.

examPoints: A scenario describing a model too large to fit in a single GPU's memory signals model parallelism rather than data parallelism.
A scenario asking to cut training cost substantially while tolerating occasional interruption signals Managed Spot Training combined with periodic checkpointing, not on-demand instances.

quiz.q: A model has grown so large that it no longer fits in a single GPU's memory even with a small batch size. Which distributed training strategy directly addresses this?
choices: Running on a single larger CPU instance
quiz.explain: Model parallelism splits the model itself, its layers or parameters, across multiple devices, which is the specific fix when the model, not just the data, is too large for one device.

quiz.q: A team wants to cut SageMaker training costs by up to 90% and is willing to tolerate occasional training interruptions as long as work isn't lost. What configuration achieves this safely?
choices: Managed Spot Training with periodic checkpointing
The largest available on-demand instance type
Restarting training from scratch after every interruption
quiz.explain: Managed Spot Training provides the cost discount, and checkpointing ensures an interrupted job resumes rather than restarting, together delivering safe cost savings.

days.recap: SageMaker training jobs run on ephemeral managed instances, distributed training splits either data (data parallelism) or the model itself (model parallelism) across devices, Managed Spot Training with checkpointing cuts cost safely, and File/Pipe/FastFile input modes trade off startup latency against simplicity.

days.title: Hyperparameter Optimization with SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning

concepts.heading: What Automatic Model Tuning Does
concepts.body: SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning (HPO) runs many training jobs across a defined range of hyperparameters, automatically searching for the combination that optimizes a chosen objective metric such as validation accuracy or F1-score. Rather than a data scientist manually guessing and re-running training with different settings, HPO systematically explores the hyperparameter space and reports the best-performing combination along with the full history of every trial for later inspection. This is one of the clearest examples of SageMaker automating a traditionally manual, trial-and-error-heavy part of the ML workflow. HPO integrates with any SageMaker training job, whether built-in algorithm or custom container.

concepts.heading: Search Strategies: Bayesian, Random, Grid, and Hyperband
concepts.body: HPO supports several search strategies with different efficiency tradeoffs: Grid Search exhaustively tries every combination in the specified ranges, guaranteeing the best combination within the grid but scaling exponentially with the number of hyperparameters; Random Search samples combinations randomly, which is cheaper than grid search and often surprisingly competitive; Bayesian Optimization builds a probabilistic model of how hyperparameters affect the objective metric based on prior trials and uses that model to intelligently choose the next combination to try, generally finding good results with fewer total trials; and Hyperband allocates a small budget to many configurations and aggressively terminates poor performers early. Exam questions emphasizing efficient search that learns from previous trials point to Bayesian optimization specifically.

concepts.heading: Warm Start Tuning
concepts.body: Warm Start tuning lets a new HPO job reuse the results of a previous, related tuning job as a starting point rather than exploring the hyperparameter space from zero knowledge, which speeds convergence and reduces the number of training jobs needed when tuning a similar problem repeatedly, for example retuning a model periodically as new data arrives, or tuning a slightly modified version of a previously tuned model. There are two warm start types: identical data and algorithm reuse, and transfer learning reuse across a changed algorithm or dataset. This capability turns tuning into a cumulative, ongoing process rather than a one-off exercise repeated from scratch every time.

concepts.heading: Balancing Concurrency, Cost, and Tuning Quality
concepts.body: HPO jobs are configured with a maximum number of total training jobs and a maximum number of jobs run concurrently, and both settings trade off wall-clock time against cost and tuning quality: running many jobs concurrently finishes tuning faster but, for Bayesian optimization specifically, limits how much the search can learn from earlier results before launching new trials, since concurrent jobs can't benefit from each other's still-in-progress outcomes. In practice, teams balance a modest concurrency level against total budget to let Bayesian search actually improve over time while still completing in a reasonable timeframe. This tradeoff is a nuanced but recurring exam theme distinguishing fastest tuning from most sample-efficient tuning.

examPoints: A scenario emphasizing efficient hyperparameter search that learns from prior trial results, minimizing wasted compute, signals Bayesian Optimization (or Hyperband for early termination of poor trials) rather than grid or random search.
A scenario describing reuse of a previous, similar tuning job's results to speed up a new tuning job signals Warm Start tuning.

quiz.q: A team wants to search a hyperparameter space efficiently by having each new trial informed by the results of previous trials, minimizing wasted training runs. Which HPO strategy fits best?
quiz.explain: Bayesian Optimization builds a probabilistic model from prior trial outcomes to intelligently select the next hyperparameter combination, unlike grid search's exhaustive and uninformed approach.

quiz.q: A team has already tuned a very similar model on comparable data and wants a new tuning job to start faster by leveraging that prior work. What should they use?
choices: Start the search completely from scratch
quiz.explain: Warm Start tuning explicitly reuses results from a previous, related tuning job as a starting point, accelerating convergence for the new job.

days.recap: Automatic Model Tuning automates hyperparameter search toward an objective metric using Bayesian optimization, random search, grid search, or Hyperband, Warm Start reuses prior tuning results, and concurrency settings trade off speed against Bayesian search quality.

days.title: Evaluating Model Performance: Classification and Regression Metrics

concepts.heading: Precision, Recall, and F1-Score
concepts.body: Accuracy alone can be dangerously misleading on imbalanced datasets, since a model that always predicts the majority class can score a high accuracy while being useless for the minority class that actually matters. Precision measures what fraction of positive predictions were actually correct, relevant when false positives are costly, recall measures what fraction of actual positives the model successfully caught, relevant when false negatives are costly, and F1-score is the harmonic mean of the two, useful as a single balanced metric when both error types matter. Choosing which of these to optimize for depends entirely on the relative business cost of false positives versus false negatives in the specific use case being modeled.

concepts.heading: The Confusion Matrix and Cost-Sensitive Metric Selection
concepts.body: A confusion matrix breaks predictions into true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives, making it possible to reason concretely about the cost of each error type for a specific business problem. In fraud detection, a false negative (missing actual fraud) is typically far more costly than a false positive (flagging a legitimate transaction for review), so recall is usually prioritized; in a spam filter, a false positive (blocking a legitimate email) is often more disruptive than a false negative, so precision is usually prioritized. The exam consistently tests this asymmetric-cost reasoning rather than assuming one metric is universally better.

concepts.heading: AUC-ROC for Threshold-Independent Evaluation
concepts.body: AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) summarizes a classifier's ability to distinguish between classes across all possible decision thresholds, rather than at just one fixed threshold, with a value near 1.0 indicating excellent separation and 0.5 indicating no better than random guessing. This threshold-independent view is useful when the final decision threshold hasn't been chosen yet, or when comparing two models' fundamental discriminative power before deciding where to set the operating threshold for the business. AUC-ROC can be misleadingly optimistic on severely imbalanced datasets, where Precision-Recall AUC is often a more informative alternative.

concepts.heading: Regression Metrics: RMSE, MAE, and R-squared
concepts.body: For regression problems, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) squares errors before averaging, making it disproportionately sensitive to large individual errors and outliers; Mean Absolute Error (MAE) averages the absolute value of errors, treating all error magnitudes proportionally and making it more robust to outliers than RMSE; and R-squared (the coefficient of determination) reports the proportion of variance in the target variable that the model explains, with 1.0 indicating a perfect fit and 0 indicating no better than predicting the mean. RMSE is preferred when large errors are especially undesirable and should be penalized more heavily, while MAE is preferred when a more evenly weighted view of error magnitude is desired.

examPoints: A scenario stating that missing an actual positive case (a false negative) is the most costly error, such as in fraud or disease detection, signals prioritizing recall over precision or plain accuracy.

A scenario noting that a model achieves very high accuracy on a severely imbalanced dataset should raise suspicion that accuracy is misleading, and the fix is to also examine F1-score, precision/recall, or AUC-ROC.

quiz.q: In a medical screening model, failing to flag an actual disease case (a false negative) is far more dangerous than a false alarm (a false positive). Which metric should be prioritized?
quiz.explain: Recall measures how well the model captures actual positive cases, directly addressing the cost of missing them, whereas accuracy can be misleading and R-squared/MAE are regression metrics, not applicable here.

quiz.q: A highly imbalanced dataset (1% positive class) produces a model with 99% accuracy that actually predicts the negative class for every single example. What does this reveal?
choices: Accuracy alone can be misleading on imbalanced data and should be supplemented with metrics like F1-score or recall
Recall is always high when accuracy is high
quiz.explain: This scenario is the classic illustration of accuracy's blind spot on imbalanced data — additional metrics are needed to reveal that the model isn't actually detecting the minority class at all.

days.recap: Precision and recall trade off differently depending on which error type is costlier, F1-score balances both, AUC-ROC evaluates discrimination across thresholds, and RMSE/MAE/R-squared serve the analogous role for regression models.

days.title: Overfitting, Underfitting, and Regularization Techniques

concepts.heading: Recognizing Overfitting and Underfitting
concepts.body: Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data's noise and idiosyncrasies so closely that it fails to generalize to new data, revealed by a large gap between high training accuracy and much lower validation accuracy. Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple to capture even the underlying patterns in the training data, revealed by both training and validation accuracy being low and similar to each other. Distinguishing between the two is the essential first diagnostic step before choosing a fix, since the appropriate remedy is nearly opposite in each case. The exam consistently frames a big train/validation gap as overfitting and both low as underfitting.

concepts.heading: Regularization: L1 and L2 Penalties
concepts.body: Regularization techniques add a penalty term to the loss function that discourages overly large model weights, which reduces a model's tendency to fit noise. L1 (Lasso) regularization penalizes the absolute value of weights and tends to drive some weights exactly to zero, effectively performing automatic feature selection. L2 (Ridge) regularization penalizes the squared value of weights and shrinks all weights toward zero somewhat evenly without eliminating any entirely, which is generally preferred when most features are believed to carry at least some signal. The strength of regularization is itself a tunable hyperparameter, and too much regularization can push a model from overfitting into underfitting.

concepts.heading: Dropout and Early Stopping
concepts.body: Dropout, common in neural networks, randomly deactivates a fraction of neurons during each training step, forcing the network to learn more robust, redundant representations rather than relying too heavily on any single neuron or feature path. Early stopping monitors validation performance during training and halts training once validation performance stops improving, even as training performance continues to improve, directly preventing the model from continuing to overfit past its optimal point. Both techniques are typically used together with other regularization methods rather than as standalone solutions, and both require a validation set that is monitored during, not just after, training.

concepts.heading: Fixing Underfitting
concepts.body: Underfitting is addressed by increasing model capacity, adding more layers or units to a neural network, using a more expressive algorithm, or adding more informative features, training for longer if the model hasn't converged, or reducing regularization strength if it's currently too aggressive for the amount of available data. It's important not to reflexively apply overfitting fixes, like adding regularization, to an underfitting problem, since that would make an already-too-simple model even less expressive. The exam tests this distinction directly by describing a low-training-accuracy scenario and offering a regularization-based distractor as the wrong answer.

examPoints: A scenario describing near-perfect training accuracy alongside much lower validation accuracy signals overfitting, with regularization, dropout, or early stopping as the fix.
A scenario describing both training and validation accuracy being low signals underfitting, with increasing model complexity or training duration as the fix, not adding more regularization.

quiz.q: A model achieves 98% training accuracy but only 65% validation accuracy. What is the most likely issue and appropriate fix?
choices: Overfitting; apply regularization, dropout, or early stopping
This is normal and requires no action
quiz.explain: The large gap between training and validation accuracy is the defining signature of overfitting, and regularization, dropout, or early stopping are the standard remedies.

quiz.q: A model shows low accuracy on both the training set and the validation set. What should be done to address this underfitting?
choices: Increase model complexity or add more informative features
quiz.explain: Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern, so increasing its capacity or feature richness is the correct direction, not adding more regularization.

days.recap: A large training-vs-validation gap signals overfitting (fixed with regularization, dropout, or early stopping), while low performance on both signals underfitting (fixed by increasing model capacity), and L1 versus L2 regularization differ in whether they zero out weights entirely or shrink them evenly.

days.title: Governing Models with Model Registry and Tracking Experiments

concepts.heading: SageMaker Model Registry for Versioning and Approval
concepts.body: SageMaker Model Registry catalogs trained model versions within model package groups and tracks an approval status for each — Pending, Approved, or Rejected — turning deployment into a governed workflow rather than an ad hoc action, where only models that have been explicitly reviewed and approved can be promoted to production. This creates an auditable record of exactly which model version is running in production at any time and who approved it. Model Registry integrates directly with SageMaker Pipelines, so a pipeline's final step is commonly register this candidate model and a separate approval step gates the subsequent deployment step.

concepts.heading: SageMaker Experiments for Tracking Training Runs
concepts.body: SageMaker Experiments automatically captures and organizes the hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts of every training run, grouping related runs into experiments and trials so that dozens or hundreds of tuning attempts can be compared side by side without manually logging results in a spreadsheet. This is especially valuable during hyperparameter tuning or iterative model development, where losing track of which configuration produced which result quickly becomes unmanageable at scale. Experiments integrates with SageMaker Studio's visual interface for filtering, sorting, and charting runs against each other. A scenario describing systematic comparison of many training runs' configurations and results is describing Experiments.

concepts.heading: Model Lineage Tracking for Reproducibility and Audit
concepts.body: Model lineage tracking records the full chain connecting a specific model back to the exact dataset, preprocessing code, training code, and hyperparameters that produced it, which is essential both for reproducibility and for auditability in regulated industries that must demonstrate how a production decision-making model was created. Without lineage tracking, answering what data and code produced this specific model artifact currently running in production can become forensic guesswork months after the fact. SageMaker automatically captures much of this lineage when training jobs, processing jobs, and pipelines are used consistently through the SageMaker SDK.

concepts.heading: Reducing Duplicate Work Across Teams
concepts.body: When multiple data scientists or teams work on related models, using Model Registry and Experiments together prevents duplicated effort: Experiments makes it easy to check whether a similar hyperparameter configuration has already been tried, and Model Registry makes it easy to see whether a suitable approved model already exists before spending compute training a near-duplicate from scratch. This organizational benefit compounds as a company's ML practice matures and more teams share underlying infrastructure and datasets. The exam frames systematically comparing many experiments as Experiments and governing which model version gets deployed as Model Registry, two related but distinct capabilities that are easy to confuse.

examPoints: A scenario requiring that only reviewed and approved model versions can reach production, with a clear governance workflow, signals SageMaker Model Registry.
A scenario requiring systematic comparison of hyperparameters and metrics across dozens of training runs signals SageMaker Experiments.

quiz.q: A company requires that a model can only be deployed to production after a designated reviewer has explicitly approved that specific model version. Which service enforces this workflow?
choices: Deploy all models immediately without review
SageMaker Model Registry with its approval status workflow
quiz.explain: Model Registry's Pending/Approved/Rejected status workflow is specifically designed to gate deployment behind explicit review and approval.

quiz.q: A data science team has run dozens of training jobs with different hyperparameters and needs to systematically compare their configurations and resulting metrics. What should they use?
choices: Manually record results in a spreadsheet
quiz.explain: Experiments automatically tracks and organizes the hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts of every run for systematic comparison, unlike manual spreadsheet tracking.

days.recap: Model Registry governs which model versions reach production through an approval workflow, Experiments tracks and compares training runs at scale, and lineage tracking ties a production model back to the exact data and code that produced it for reproducibility and audit.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Model Development and Evaluation

concepts.heading: The Domain 2 Model Development Pipeline
concepts.body: Domain 2 traces a model from initial approach selection through governance: choosing a modeling approach, running and optimizing training jobs including distributed training and Spot training, tuning hyperparameters automatically, evaluating performance with the right metrics for the problem, diagnosing and fixing overfitting or underfitting, and governing model versions and experiment history. At 26% of the exam, Domain 2 is nearly as heavily weighted as Domain 1, and scenario questions frequently combine two of these stages, for example describing an overfitting symptom that arose during a specific HPO configuration.

concepts.heading: Metric Selection Is the Recurring Skill
concepts.body: Across Domain 2, the single most tested skill is correctly matching an evaluation metric to the cost structure of the business problem described: recall when missing positives is costly, precision when false alarms are costly, F1 for balanced concerns, AUC-ROC for threshold-independent comparison, and RMSE versus MAE depending on how heavily large regression errors should be penalized. A large fraction of Domain 2 wrong answers substitute a plausible-sounding but wrong metric, for instance offering accuracy as a distractor whenever the scenario describes an imbalanced dataset.

concepts.heading: Overfitting/Underfitting Diagnosis as a Gateway Skill
concepts.body: Correctly identifying overfitting versus underfitting from a described symptom, a large train/validation gap versus both scores being low, is a gateway skill that then determines which entire category of fix is appropriate: reducing model capacity/variance versus increasing it. Getting this initial diagnosis backwards leads directly to selecting a plausible-sounding but opposite-direction wrong answer, which is one of the more common trap patterns in this domain.

concepts.heading: From Baseline to Governed, Production-Ready Model
concepts.body: Zooming out, Domain 2 traces a model's journey from a first working baseline to something an organization can trust: pick an approach that matches problem standardization and team expertise, train it efficiently using distributed or Spot infrastructure, tune it systematically rather than by guesswork, judge it against a metric that reflects the real business cost of errors, diagnose and correct its generalization behavior, and finally catalog and govern the result so it can be safely promoted. Holding this end-to-end arc in mind turns six days of separate topics into one coherent narrative about turning a rough model into a production-ready asset.

examPoints: When a Domain 2 scenario describes a train/validation performance gap, immediately classify it as overfitting first, since that classification determines the entire remaining direction of the answer.

When a Domain 2 scenario mentions cost asymmetry between error types (missing a positive vs. a false alarm), that phrase is almost always pointing at recall vs. precision, respectively, rather than accuracy.

quiz.q: Which condition describes overfitting rather than underfitting?
choices: Both training and validation performance are low
Training performance is high but validation performance is much lower
Overfitting is unrelated to training/validation comparison
quiz.explain: A large gap between high training performance and lower validation performance is the defining signature of overfitting.

quiz.q: In a spam filter, incorrectly flagging a legitimate email as spam (a false positive) is considered more costly than missing a spam email. Which metric should be prioritized?
quiz.explain: Precision measures the proportion of flagged (positive) predictions that are correct, directly addressing the cost of false positives, whereas recall addresses missed positives and RMSE is a regression metric.

days.recap: Domain 2 wraps up as modeling approach selection to training optimization (distributed/Spot) to hyperparameter tuning to metric-driven evaluation to overfitting/underfitting diagnosis to governance (Registry/Experiments), with metric selection and over/underfitting diagnosis as the two most heavily tested skills.

days.title: Choosing Inference Infrastructure: Real-Time, Serverless, Async, and Batch Endpoints

concepts.heading: Real-Time Inference Endpoints
concepts.body: A real-time SageMaker endpoint runs continuously on provisioned instances and responds to individual prediction requests with low, consistent latency, making it the right choice for interactive applications like a live recommendation widget or a fraud check that must complete within a strict time budget. Because the underlying instances run continuously whether or not requests are arriving, real-time endpoints incur cost around the clock, and capacity must be sized or auto-scaled for peak expected load. This is the default, most flexible inference option and supports features like multi-model endpoints and production variants for A/B testing, discussed later this week.

concepts.heading: Serverless Inference for Intermittent Traffic
concepts.body: Serverless Inference removes the need to provision or manage instances at all: SageMaker automatically provisions compute in response to requests and scales down to zero when there's no traffic, so cost is incurred only when requests actually arrive, ideal for workloads with unpredictable or intermittent traffic where a continuously running endpoint would sit mostly idle. The tradeoff is cold-start latency when a request arrives after a period of inactivity, since compute needs to spin up before it can process the first request. This makes Serverless Inference a poor fit for strict, consistent low-latency requirements but an excellent fit for sporadic internal tools or infrequent API calls.

concepts.heading: Asynchronous Inference for Large or Slow Requests
concepts.body: Asynchronous Inference queues incoming requests and processes them in the background, returning a reference the caller can poll rather than blocking for an immediate response, which suits workloads with large payloads or long processing times where an immediate synchronous response isn't required or even possible within typical API timeout limits. Because requests are queued, Asynchronous Inference can also scale down to zero instances during idle periods like Serverless Inference, combining cost efficiency with support for larger payloads and longer processing times than either real-time or serverless endpoints typically allow. This is the answer whenever a scenario emphasizes large files and no immediate response needed.

concepts.heading: Batch Transform for Offline Bulk Scoring
concepts.body: Batch Transform runs inference across an entire dataset at once as a standalone job, without maintaining any persistent endpoint, making it the most cost-effective option when predictions are needed periodically for large volumes of data rather than continuously for individual requests, for example scoring an entire customer database overnight rather than exposing a live endpoint that mostly sits unused. Because Batch Transform spins up resources only for the duration of the job and shuts them down afterward, it avoids paying for standing endpoint capacity entirely. The choice between Batch Transform and Asynchronous Inference usually comes down to whether the workload is a single, self-contained bulk job or an ongoing stream of individually submitted large/slow requests.

examPoints: A scenario describing highly unpredictable, intermittent traffic where paying for continuously running infrastructure would be wasteful signals Serverless Inference.

A scenario describing large payloads that don't need an immediate response signals Asynchronous Inference, while a single large periodic bulk-scoring job with no need for an endpoint at all signals Batch Transform.

quiz.q: A company's inference traffic is highly unpredictable and often drops to zero for hours at a time, and the company wants to avoid paying for idle infrastructure during those gaps. Which inference option fits best?
choices: A continuously running real-time endpoint sized for peak load
quiz.explain: Serverless Inference scales to zero and incurs no cost when there's no traffic, directly matching this unpredictable, intermittent pattern, unlike a continuously running real-time endpoint.

quiz.q: An application needs to process large document uploads where clients don't need an immediate synchronous response. Which inference option is designed for this?
quiz.explain: Asynchronous Inference queues large or slow requests and processes them in the background, which is exactly suited to large payloads that don't require an immediate response.

days.recap: Real-time endpoints suit continuous low-latency traffic, Serverless Inference suits intermittent traffic without idle cost, Asynchronous Inference suits large payloads without an immediate-response requirement, and Batch Transform suits large, periodic, offline scoring jobs with no persistent endpoint.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code for ML: CloudFormation and CDK

concepts.heading: Codifying SageMaker Resources
concepts.body: SageMaker resources — endpoints, endpoint configurations, notebook instances, training jobs, and more — can be defined declaratively in CloudFormation templates or programmatically in CDK, turning what would otherwise be manual console clicks into version-controlled, reviewable, and repeatable code. This matters because manual console configuration is error-prone and leaves no automatic audit trail of what changed and when, whereas an IaC template lives in source control alongside a pull-request review process like any other code change. Any exam scenario emphasizing reproducible or consistent ML infrastructure across environments is describing this IaC approach rather than manual setup.

concepts.heading: Endpoint Configuration as Code
concepts.body: Defining a SageMaker endpoint configuration in CloudFormation/CDK — instance type and count, auto-scaling policies, and the traffic-weight distribution across multiple production variants — makes every change to that configuration explicit and trackable through normal code review and version control, rather than a silent manual console edit that's hard to attribute or roll back. This is particularly valuable for regulated environments that need to demonstrate exactly when and why an endpoint's configuration changed. Rolling back a bad configuration change also becomes as simple as reverting the template and redeploying, rather than manually reconstructing the previous settings.

concepts.heading: Consistency Across Environments
